rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: “Those whom you claim” means those whom the disbelievers claim are gods.
rows.anchor: Those whom you claim means “those whom you claim to be gods” (JJ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told to challenge the idolaters to invoke their deities, as in 7:195, 10:38, 11:13, 17:56, and 46:4.
rows.anchor: the Prophet is commanded to challenge the disbelievers to call upon their deities here and in 7:195; 10:38; 11:13; 17:56; 46:4

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A similar challenge says those invoked possess no more than a date stone’s husk, with parallels at 7:194 and 22:73.
rows.anchor: do not possess so much as the husk of a date stone (cf. 7:194; 22:73).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge anticipates Judgment, when the alleged partners fail to answer; God is Truth and all others invoked are false.
rows.anchor: they will not answer them. And they will see the punishment—if only they had been rightly guided! (28:64)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that God has no helper among the deities answers idolaters who viewed them as intercessors and sought nearness to God through them.
rows.anchor: some of the idolaters who maintained that their idols and deities could function as intercessors

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Gather them” may refer to the gathering of all human beings.
rows.anchor: either the gathering of all human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “Gather them” may refer only to the gathering of the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: the gathering of the disbelievers.

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The angels are questioned because they are the highest beings whom idolaters attributed divinity to and worshipped.
rows.anchor: the angels are the highest of those beings to whom the idolaters had attributed divinity and whom they worshipped (R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The questioning parallels 25:17–18, where God asks whether the worshipped beings led His servants astray.
rows.anchor: Regarding the manner in which God questions the angels, 25:17 states

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: The angels' declaration that God is their Protector disavows association with those who worshipped them.
rows.anchor: the angels claim to have no bonds of association with those who worshipped them (JJ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final clause may also be read “they will not believe,” paralleling 2:6.
rows.anchor: The last phrase of v. 10 could also be read, “they will not believe.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses likewise show warnings and guidance having no effect on disbelievers.
rows.anchor: For similar verses where warnings and guidance are of no avail to disbelievers, see 7:193; 26:136; 63:6.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses remind the Prophet that he cannot guide those God has not guided and should leave them to God, as 35:8 states.
rows.anchor: These verses remind the Prophet that he cannot guide those whom God has not guided and should simply leave them to God

rows.speaker: IK, Q, R, Ṭ
rows.claim: The Reminder refers to the Quran itself, also discussed as Reminder at 36:69.
rows.anchor: The Reminder is a reference to the Quran itself (IK, Q, R,Ṭ); for the Quran as Reminder, see 36:69c.

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭs
rows.claim: “Fears the Compassionate unseen” may mean worshipping God while God remains unseen.
rows.anchor: can be interpreted as a reference to worshipping God while God remains unseen or to worshipping God in seclusion (Q, Ṭs).

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭs
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase may mean worshipping God in seclusion.
rows.anchor: can be interpreted as a reference to worshipping God while God remains unseen or to worshipping God in seclusion (Q, Ṭs).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The generous reward means Paradise or the Garden.
rows.anchor: A generous reward here means Paradise or the Garden.

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: A saying attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās says that God Himself is peace upon the people of the Garden.
rows.anchor: According to a saying attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, “God Himself is peace upon the people of the Garden” (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The saying may refer to al-Salām, Peace, as one of God's Names.
rows.anchor: one of the Names of God.

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir links the Garden's greeting of Peace to 33:44, the greeting of those who meet God.
rows.anchor: This is similar to 33:44: Their greeting on the day they meet Him will be “Peace” (IK).

rows.speaker: IK, Q
rows.claim: A hadith describes God greeting the Garden's people, who behold Him and remain absorbed in that bliss until He is unveiled to them.
rows.anchor: His Light and His Blessing remain upon them in their abodes” (IK, Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Enjoin” translates aʿhad, from the root ʿahd, whose meanings include vow, pact, or covenant.
rows.anchor: Enjoin translates aʿhad, which is from the same root as ʿahd, meaning “vow,” “pact,” or “covenant.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command recalls humanity's pre-world covenant with God: acknowledging Him as Lord means recognizing that only He deserves worship.
rows.anchor: In this sense it relates to the covenant that all human beings made with God before coming into this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran also calls Satan a manifest enemy in the cited passages.
rows.anchor: For references to Satan as a manifest enemy, also see 2:168; 2:208; 6:142; 7:22; 12:5; 17:53; 28:15; 43:62.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The straight path in this verse is cross-referenced to 1:6.
rows.anchor: For straight path, see 1:6c.

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: Al-Ṣaffāt is a Makkan sūrah believed to have been revealed immediately after al-Anʿām.
rows.anchor: A Makkan sūrah, al-Ṣaffāt is believed to have been revealed directly after Sūrah 6, al-Anʿām (JJ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah's title comes from references to angels ranged in ranks in verses 1 and 165.
rows.anchor: It takes its name from the reference to those ranged in ranks in vv. 1 and 165, both of which refer to the angels.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its stories of destroyed generations connect the sūrah to the previous one and echo 36:31's call to reflect on them.
rows.anchor: several generations or civilizations that were destroyed for rejecting God’s messengers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening verses briefly reaffirm God's Oneness and Omnipotence.
rows.anchor: After a brief reaffirmation of God’s Oneness and Omnipotence (vv. 1–5)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah describes the futility of seeking knowledge of the Unseen through jinn.
rows.anchor: describes the futility of the efforts of those who attempt to obtain knowledge of the Unseen through the jinn (vv. 6–10).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It rebukes disbelievers for rejecting God's Oneness, Muhammad's prophethood, and Resurrection, warning of their disgrace in the Hereafter and their disputes over that fate.
rows.anchor: chastises the disbelievers for rejecting the Oneness of God, the prophethood of Muhammad, and the Resurrection, warning of the ignominious end they will face in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah describes the rewards given to God's sincere servants in the Garden.
rows.anchor: the rewards God’s sincere servants receive in the Garden (vv. 40–49)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It recounts an exchange between those servants and disbelievers they knew in this world, now in Hell.
rows.anchor: the exchange they will have with the disbelievers they had known in this world, who are now in Hell (vv. 50–60).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It describes Hell's food and drink punishments, then explains the denizens' fate.
rows.anchor: punishments in the form of food and drink given to the denizens of Hell (vv.61–68)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah recounts Noah's story and the blessings God bestowed on him.
rows.anchor: accounts of several prophets and the blessings God bestowed upon them: Noah (vv. 75–82)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Abraham account includes the near sacrifice of his son.
rows.anchor: Abraham (vv. 83–113, a passage in which the near sacrifice of his son is also discussed, vv. 101–8)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Further accounts cover Moses and Aaron, Elias (Elijah), Lot, and Jonah.
rows.anchor: Moses and Aaron (vv. 114–22), Elias (Elijah; vv. 123–32), Lot (vv. 133–38), and Jonah (vv. 139–48).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only Jonah's people repent; the peoples associated with the other prophets are destroyed for rejecting God's messenger.
rows.anchor: it is only in the story of Jonah that the people repent (vv. 147–48)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah challenges the worldview of the Prophet Muhammad's contemporary idolaters.
rows.anchor: a challenge to the worldview of the idolaters of the Prophet Muhammad’s time (vv. 149–63)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It specifically refutes the divine powers idolaters attribute to angels.
rows.anchor: a refutation in particular of the Divine powers they ascribe to the angels (vv. 164–66).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conclusion addresses disbelievers and promises that the Prophet and his followers will triumph as earlier prophets did.
rows.anchor: The sūrah concludes with a final address to the disbelievers and a promise that the Prophet and his followers will triumph
